title: Digit in the Flip-and-Append Rows
statement:
Build rows of binary digits. Row 1 is 0. Each next row comes from the previous one by rewriting every digit at once: 0 becomes 01 and 1 becomes 10. So the rows start 0, 01, 0110, 01101001, …

Row n has 2^(n−1) digits. Return its k-th digit, counting from 1.
hints: Row 30 has over 500 million digits, so building it is out. Where does the k-th digit of row n come from in row n − 1?
Digit k of row n was produced by digit ⌈k / 2⌉ of row n − 1. If k is odd it is a copy of that parent; if k is even it is the flipped parent.
Walking up to row 1 flips once for every even position on the way. That count is the number of 1-bits in k − 1, so the answer is that count mod 2.

explain.intuition:
Each digit of row n − 1 produces two digits of row n: first a copy of itself, then its flip. So digit k of row n has parent ⌈k / 2⌉, and it equals the parent when k is odd and the flipped parent when k is even. Follow parents up to row 1, whose only digit is 0, and count the flips.

Switch to 0-based positions p = k − 1. Then the parent is p >> 1, and a flip happens exactly when the lowest bit of p is 1. Walking up shifts out one bit at a time, so the total number of flips is the number of 1-bits in k − 1. The answer is that count's parity, and n does not even matter.
steps: While p > 0: add p & 1 to flips and shift p right by one.
pitfalls: Building the rows as strings. Row 30 has 2²⁹ digits and runs out of time and memory.
Using k instead of k − 1 for the bit count. Position 1 must give 0 flips.
Thinking row n's second half is the reverse of the first half. It is the flipped first half.

solutions.title: Build every row
solutions.idea: Apply the rewrite rule n − 1 times and read the k-th digit. Only feasible for small n.

solutions.title: Follow the parent up
solutions.idea: Digit k comes from digit ⌈k / 2⌉ of the row above, flipped when k is even. Recurse until row 1.

solutions.title: Parity of set bits
solutions.idea: Each 1-bit in k − 1 is one flip on the way up. Count them and take the parity.

followups: Return how many 1s appear among the first k digits of row n.
The rule becomes 0 → 011 and 1 → 100. How does the parent formula change?
